newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels slip fighters into Lima - Military.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels slip fighters into Lima - Military.

text.p: A Peruvian Marxist rebel group has slipped 50 fighters into Lima to lend armed support to comrades holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's home for three months, according to a military intelligence report.

The report, obtained by Reuters on Thursday and dated Feb. 21, said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) backup fighters, led by a woman rebel leader with the nom de guerre "La Gringa," arrived in Peru's capital from strongholds in the central jungle.

The fighters would be used to carry out attacks on government and diplomatic posts in Lima as a way to support the hostage-takers, according to the report, which was sent to Armed Forces chief Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza Rios.

"We do not rule out possible alternative plans to attack and take hostages in other diplomatic sites, the Palace of Justice, Attorney General's Office and diverse public offices and private entities," the report said.

"Moreover, they may try to take international press and other mass communication media offices in order to ... take advantage of the presence in the country of more than 2,000 foreign journalists," it said.
The report did not say when the rebels were infiltrated into Lima.
But local newspaper La Republica and T.V. station America Television said on Thursday that the rebels were brought to Lima in the weeks following the Dec. 17 takeover of the residence.
They said "La Gringa," also known as "Comrade Gladys," was the military head of the mission.
Military officials were not available late on Thursday to comment on the intelligence or news reports.

A separate secret anti-terrorist police report, also obtained by Reuters, added that the rebels may try to kidnap or extort money from businessmen and foreigners linked to the government and attack the homes of cabinet ministers, diplomats, congressmen, mayors and politicians.

The guerrillas may try to seize the offices of public and private entities, especially those financed by foreign capital, and carry out acts of agitation and provocation to bolster their demand for the liberation of their jailed comrades, the report said.
The police report, dated Feb. 28, based its conclusions on intelligence data from the armed forces.

MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said on Thursday the group has not carried out attacks since about 20 rebels stormed the Japanese diplomatic compound on Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests, most of whom were released in the following days.
But the group said it has reserved the right to do so, warning that it would hit military and economic targets if security forces tried to storm the mansion.

Both the MRTA and the Peruvian government have said they want a peaceful end to Latin America's longest hostage siege. But talks to end the crisis are stalled on the rebels main and President Alberto Fujimori has said he will not hestitate to use force if the hostages are harmed.

The military report said it had detected one shipment of 12 rifles to Lima and the possible presence in the capital of one of the MRTA's most experienced fighters, who would lead the rebels' operations around the residence.
